Pioneer 10

Built for a 21-month trip to Jupiter. It kept going for more than 30 years.

Abandoned but Not Forgotten: scroll to follow its story

First to the outer planets

On March 2, 1972, an Atlas Centaur with a third stage (a solid motor modified from the Surveyor lander) lifted Pioneer 10 from Cape Canaveral. It reached a speed faster than any human-made object before it.

0
km/h, top speed

Controllers made two course corrections, on March 7 and March 26.

Through the asteroid belt

On July 15, 1972, Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to enter the asteroid belt. It came out in February 1973 after a long crossing, and met fewer hits than scientists feared. It also measured the glow of zodiacal light.

0
million km through the belt

Jupiter’s radiation wall

On November 26, 1973, the solar wind dropped and the temperature jumped a hundredfold. Pioneer 10 had hit Jupiter’s bow shock and entered its magnetosphere.

By December 1 its pictures were already better than any taken from Earth. A command and its reply now took up to 92 minutes.

Closest approach

At 02:26 UT on December 4, 1973, Pioneer 10 raced past Jupiter at about 126,000 km/h. It photographed Callisto, Ganymede and Europa, but not Io, because radiation had knocked out its photopolarimeter.

0
km from Jupiter
0
pictures, Great Red Spot included

Power from the atom

Far from the Sun, solar panels are useless. Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to run on all-nuclear electrical power, from two SNAP-19 generators that turn the heat of radioactive material into electricity.

0
watts at Jupiter

Of its 11 instruments, 6 worked continuously through the encounter.

Past Saturn and Neptune

In February 1976 it crossed Saturn’s orbit and found that Jupiter’s magnetic tail, almost 800 million km long, stretches the whole way there.

On June 13, 1983, it crossed Neptune’s orbit, then the outermost planet, and became the first human-made object to go beyond it.

A fading voice

Routine contact ended on March 31, 1997 for budget reasons. In February 1998 Voyager 1 overtook it as the farthest human-made object. Pioneer 10’s last signal came on January 23, 2003, when its power source had decayed too far to transmit.

0
billion km away
0
hours 20 min for the signal to arrive

A message for strangers

Pioneer 10 carries an aluminium plaque with a man and a woman, the solar system, and the Sun’s position relative to 14 pulsars. Any intelligent finder could work out where, and when, it came from.

Still travelling

By November 2017 it was about 118.8 AU from Earth, second only to Voyager 1. It heads toward the red star Aldebaran, the eye of Taurus, and will pass it in about two million years.

0
